data.title: Choose the correct answer for each question.
data.description: Practise must, might, may, could and can't to express certainty, possibility and deduction.
learningPoints: Use must for a strong positive deduction.
Use can't for a strong negative deduction.
Use may, might and could for possibility.
Use modal + base verb for present deductions.
Use modal + be for deductions about states.
Choose the modal according to how certain the speaker is.

sections.explain: MUST can show that the speaker is very sure something is true.

words.word: The lights are on, so they must be at home.
The lights are on, so they might definitely be at home.
The lights are on, so they must to be at home.

sections.explain: CAN'T can show that the speaker is sure something is not true.

words.word: He can't be at work; I just saw him here.
He mustn't be at work; I just saw him here.
He can't to be at work; I just saw him here.
She might come to the party later.
She might to come to the party later.
She must come to the party later, maybe.

sections.explain: MAY can express a possible situation.

words.word: It may rain this afternoon.
It may to rain this afternoon.
It may rains this afternoon.

sections.explain: COULD can express a possible explanation or future event.

words.word: This could be the right address.
This could to be the right address.
This could is the right address.

sections.explain: Use MUST for strong certainty and MIGHT/MAY/COULD for weaker possibility.

words.word: He knows every answer; he must be very well prepared.
He knows every answer; he can't be prepared.
He knows every answer; he might certainly be prepared.

sections.explain: MIGHT NOT expresses that something is possibly not true or may not happen.

words.word: They might not know about the change.
They don't might know about the change.
They might don't know about the change.

sections.summary: Using a modal before a state verb.
sections.explain: A modal is followed by the base form, including BE.

words.word: That must be expensive.
That must is expensive.
That must to be expensive.

sections.explain: For a strong negative deduction, use CAN'T rather than MUSTN'T.

words.word: That can't be Sarah; she's abroad.
That mustn't be Sarah; she's abroad.
That can't Sarah be; she's abroad.

sections.explain: Use MIGHT, MAY or COULD when the evidence is uncertain.

words.word: I don't know where Tom is. He might be at the gym.
I don't know where Tom is. He must be at the gym, perhaps.
I don't know where Tom is. He might is at the gym.
